what_it_does: Zero-knowledge proofs are a cryptographic technique that lets one party convince another they know a secret without revealing the secret itself — used, for example, in privacy-preserving blockchains. This paper shows that a well-known hardware attack called RowHammer — which repeatedly accesses rows in a memory chip (DRAM) until electrical interference causes a neighboring row to randomly flip its stored bits — can be used to corrupt the arithmetic inside a zero-knowledge proof. By carefully inducing those bit flips into the exponent values used during proof generation, and then analyzing the resulting broken proofs using a mathematical tool called bilinear pairing (a structured way to check relationships between cryptographic numbers), the attacker can recover the secret values the proof was supposed to hide. This is a novel demonstration that software-level cryptographic security can be undermined by physical hardware vulnerabilities, though the practicality under real-world conditions would require verification beyond the abstract.
